story_text.value:
What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering for a while, and finally was able to prototype thanks to AI coding agents.

erXos is a capability-based microkernel OS in Erlang: drivers, filesystems, and the network stack are all supervised Erlang processes, same as any app.

The kernel itself is Fiasco, in C++, slightly modified for erXos needs. This is an OS I wanted for a long time: an Erlang machine where every BEAM process is a process visible to the OS and scheduler, not something bolted on top.

You can try it right now with nothing to install: there is an emulator on the website that boots the whole OS in the browser ARM64 emulator. At the rc prompt, try `ps`, `top`, `ping` or `erl` and write any kind of erlang code. There's a Pi 4 SD image and a QEMU image too. The goal is to build an ultra-reliable microkernel OS with hot code loading and both system and BEAM-based isolation. The latter is one thing that would allow you to run millions of processes on the system, something that would be prohibitive on a microkernel alone due to the context switch overhead. Capabilities keep every component least-privileged, supervision keeps the machine running when drivers or subsystems crash, and hot code loading would let you fix a broken driver without reboot.

The secondary goal is to keep as much of a UNIX face as possible. Too many novel OSes change things for no particular reason that makes them hard to use. erXos tries to preserve as many existing UNIX/FreeBSD concepts as much as possible to remove the learning curve.

What works today:

- Boots in the browser/v64, in QEMU, and on a Raspberry Pi 4 from an SD card

- A real shell (plan9 rc) with job control, pipes, `ps`, `grep`. It feels like UNIX on the surface

- Erlang versions of basic UNIX apps.

- Drivers written in Erlang: UART, virtio, SD card, Ethernet (GENET), display

- A pure Erlang EROFS filesystem for root images

- A TCP/IP stack in Erlang based on FreeBSD network stack and verified for correctness against it

- Domains: every app runs as its own address space or Erlang node, isolated from others

- Plan 9 namespaces and 9P everywhere; windows are files like RIO and 9P is a file protocol between OS servers

- Supervision end to end: if a driver fails, its supervisor resets the device and restarts it

I also have 2 demo apps built on app sdk: a full-screen kiosk app with live crypto quotes and clock and, of course Doom, which ships on the Pi 4 card image (type `doom`).

What's coming:

- Raspberry Pi 5 support

- Full display on the Pi

- WIFI

- Bluetooth

- POSIX-lite for C programs, so existing code can run as a domain

- Performance, debugging and tracing features.

The code is all available under the BSD license.

Would love to hear all and any feedback!

story_text.value:
When I used to code without AI (probably not even one year ago), I sometimes reached a state of "flow" and it truly was a great feeling. Nowadays, I rarely code from scratch and most of my development (at work, at least) comes through AI.

I get it that I can still code "the old way" in my free time, but I'm more curious to understand if people in a similar situation can reach the same state by vibe/AI coding, and how.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Sachin, and I’ve spent the last couple of months working on Faros Desktop, a Mac app that visualizes how you use your local AI coding tools into one place and then makes recommendations to make your subscription spend go further.

As agents have replaced hands-on-keyboard work, the team and I wanted to better understand what’s in our session traces. Faros Desktop hydrates with on-device session history in Codex, Claude Code, Github Copilot, and Cursor to let users deep dive into a beautiful visualization of AI session traces. Then based on consolidating that information, the app shows patterns in usage as well as recommendations for ways to save spend through simple changes that we call Power Ups.

Faros Desktop is totally free, with no login required and no API keys needed. The app also only uses on-device models to summarize local sessions in chunks, then organizes them by project and task. You can jump around a session timeline and see exactly the messages and tool calls in the trace.

The business model here for Faros Desktop is to drive thought leadership and create leads for our sales team to sell the company’s multi-player Token Engineering Platform for large engineering organizations. Faros has been serving large engineering organizations for the past seven years, so it was cool to be able to build a product for all Builders, not just enterprise engineering orgs.

One big direction we’re exploring: using previous sessions to make the next one better. We’re looking at local memory portability across harnesses as well as multi-player modes to share memory within your direct team. I’d love to hear thoughts on that.

Docs and product walkthrough: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/ Setup: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/getting-started/install-and-se... Data handling: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/settings-and-privacy/understan... Faros website: https://www.faros.ai/

story_text.value:
I've noticed the same pattern across three different Claude-coded projects now. Initial velocity is strong, but starts to fade until returns are negative.

It seems a combination of changes in model behavior and increasing code base size—emphasis on the latter. The larger the code base and documented history/progress (e.g. through updates to completed work and instructions, as in .md files), the more drift starts to set in.

At a certain point, you get collapse. This is where it can't maintain consistency within a single unit of work. It can manifest, for example, as adding a similar element to a view, but styling it in a completely different manner than existing elements. It literally feels random.

It can also manifest as incoherent or poorly implemented logic and behavior. I've followed different advice, restructured projects, entered plan mode, added deterministic checks, styles, rules, etc. But, it feels like whack-a-mole and it's unclear that it actually adheres to these rules in the first place.

Then, there's the question of it moving the problem. In response to my complaints of inconsistent UI generation, it recommended a style check to run after its UI changes. Of course, that begs the question of why it doesn't just apply those rules in the initial generation.

But, I am at a place now where it spins up AI agents to do a full UI/UX review—Playwright and all. Yet, it's still drifting and not catching it. This is consistent with its unit tests—on my latest project it has now generated a suite of hundreds of somewhat time consuming tests that it constantly runs pre-commit, and not a single test has ever failed. Meanwhile, there have been a number of bugs. When questioned, it said it had been testing the "wrong layer" and had essentially generated self-confirming tests.

My question is who is really winning here? When querying Google, it points to so many claims of success and approaches that supposedly contribute to that success. But, when you break down the underlying source for those claims, it appears to be largely Reddit.

Yet, pressing it further reveals that virtually every actual study shows either little to no productivity gains or actual regression—particularly where experienced engineers are concerned. And some of those studies debunk the self-reported claims of exactly the kind you see on Reddit, etc.

So, who here has developed a quality production application of any complexity using AI coding? If anyone, which harness/model, and what techniques did you use? Also, can you point us to your repo?

title.value: Ask HN: Who's really winning with AI-Coding?
